criteria.text: A committed instruction file exists: is true
criteria.title: An instruction file is committed
criteria.fix: Commit a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md that tells an agent how this repository works.
criteria.why: Without one, an agent starts every task by guessing how the repository builds, tests and is laid out, and those guesses drive its first changes.

criteria.text: Instruction files name a check command: is above 0
criteria.title: An instruction file names a check command
criteria.fix: Name the command that checks a change (for example make check) in your instruction file.
criteria.why: An agent can confirm its change only if it knows which command checks it. A named command that resolves saves it guessing, and running the wrong check or none.

criteria.text: Instruction claims that do not hold: is 0
criteria.title: Every checkable instruction claim holds
criteria.fix: Update the instruction lines whose claims no longer match the repository.
criteria.why: An agent takes its instructions literally. A line saying a script runs in CI, or a version is pinned, that is no longer true sends it the wrong way with full confidence.

criteria.text: Always-loaded Claude Code instruction lines: is at most 200
criteria.title: Always-loaded instructions fit in 200 lines
criteria.fix: Move detail that is needed only sometimes into files the instructions point to.
criteria.why: Always-loaded text is read on every task and competes with the task for the agent's attention. Long files bury the rules that matter.

criteria.text: Observability rung: is at least 1
criteria.title: Some runtime telemetry is committed
criteria.fix: Add a telemetry dependency, a runbook or an OBSERVABILITY.md so an agent can see the system run.
criteria.why: Telemetry in the code is what any view of the running system is built on. Without it, there is nothing for an agent or a person to read when checking how a change behaves in use.

criteria.text: Observability rung: is at least 3
criteria.title: Runtime telemetry reaches rung 3
criteria.fix: Give agents a way to read logs or metrics, such as a logs or metrics MCP server or skill.
criteria.why: When an agent can query logs or metrics itself, it can check a change against the running system instead of handing that back to a person.

criteria.text: Import-graph modularity: is at least 0.3
criteria.title: The import graph has module structure
criteria.fix: Group related modules into packages that mostly import within themselves.
criteria.why: Clear modules let an agent load the part of the code a task touches, instead of tracing the whole repository to change one thing.

criteria.text: Cross-package imports: is above 0
criteria.title: Packages import one another
criteria.fix: Nothing to change on its own: this is met once one package imports another.
criteria.why: A guard for the next condition: with no import between packages, the front-door share reads null by default and says nothing about how packages are entered.

criteria.text: Cross-package imports through a package's front door: is at least 0.9
criteria.title: Cross-package imports use a package's front door
criteria.fix: Import other packages through their public API rather than their submodules.
criteria.why: When packages are entered through one public surface, an agent can change a package's insides without breaking callers it never read.

rows.title: Linters run in CI, suppression cap

criteria.text: A CI line runs a linter on ordinary changes and can stop its job: is true
criteria.title: CI runs a linter or type checker
criteria.fix: Add a CI step that runs your linter (ruff check ., eslint, mypy, make lint) on pull requests, without || true, continue-on-error or allow_failure.
criteria.why: A linter or type checker in CI catches mechanical mistakes in every change, an agent's included, before a reviewer spends time on them.

criteria.text: Stale suppression comments: is at most 10
criteria.title: Stale suppressions stay at 10 or fewer
criteria.fix: Revisit the oldest suppression comments and fix or remove them.
criteria.why: A suppression that survives many edits switches a check off in code that keeps changing, and an agent editing nearby gets no sign the warning still matters.

criteria.text: Marker aging is reliable: is true
criteria.title: Suppression ages can be read from history
criteria.fix: Run on a full clone so suppression ages can be measured.
criteria.why: A guard for the suppression count: on a shallow or squashed history every suppression looks new, so a count of 0 would say nothing.

criteria.text: Ownership-map patterns naming a module path: is above 0
criteria.title: A boundary or ownership map names a module path
criteria.fix: Commit a CODEOWNERS line per module path, or an ARCHITECTURE.md that names module paths.
criteria.why: A map that names module paths tells an agent which code belongs together, and with CODEOWNERS, whose review a change there needs.

criteria.text: Production source file size at the 95th percentile: is at most 500
criteria.title: 95% of production source files are 500 lines or fewer
criteria.fix: Split the largest files along their natural seams.
criteria.why: With nearly all source files at 500 lines or fewer, an agent can read a whole file before editing it, rather than a slice. Tests and fixtures are counted apart, so many small ones cannot hide a large source file.

rows.title: CI and the agent's local check

criteria.text: A CI check runs on ordinary changes and can stop its job: is true
criteria.title: CI runs your tests or linters, and an error stops the job
criteria.fix: Add a CI step that runs your test or lint command on pull requests, without || true, continue-on-error or allow_failure.
criteria.why: This turns "the agent says it works" into "CI says it works": a check that can stop its job runs on ordinary changes, so a broken change turns the job red where everyone can see it.

criteria.text: Dependency manifests without a committed lockfile: is 0
criteria.title: Every dependency manifest has its lockfile
criteria.fix: Commit the lockfile for each dependency manifest (or pin a requirements file with ==), so an agent installs what CI tests. A Gradle version catalog or NuGet central package management pins direct versions only: turn on dependency locking.
criteria.why: A committed lockfile means an agent installs the dependency versions CI tested, so a local test result matches CI's.

criteria.text: CI runs a coverage gate of at least 50 percent: is true
criteria.title: CI runs a coverage gate of at least 50 percent
criteria.fix: Set a fail_under (or your tool's threshold) of at least 50 percent, written as a number, near your current coverage. Run the coverage check in a CI step on pull requests (pytest --cov, not plain pytest), without || true or continue-on-error. Then CI keeps coverage at the level you have reached.
criteria.why: An enforced floor turns the job red when a change takes coverage below it, so tests an agent removes or skips show in CI instead of passing quietly.

criteria.text: A mutation run completed: is true
criteria.title: A mutation run has completed
criteria.fix: Run the opt-in mutation pass to see which tests pin behaviour.
criteria.why: Coverage shows tests run the code; a mutation run shows whether they notice it changing. A completed run names the surviving mutants, which are the tests an agent cannot yet rely on.

criteria.text: Review evidence exists: is true
criteria.title: Changes get reviewed
criteria.fix: Commit an AI review step in CI, or review merged changes before they land.
criteria.why: A second reader, a person or a review agent, catches what an agent misunderstood about intent, which tests and linters do not look for.

criteria.text: Share of merged changes reviewed: is at least 0.8
criteria.title: Most merged changes are reviewed
criteria.fix: Aim for a review on at least four in five merged changes.
criteria.why: Review protects only the changes it reaches. At four in five merged changes, most of what lands, an agent's work included, has had a second reader.

criteria.text: Share of merged changes approved: is at least 0.5
criteria.title: Half of merged changes are approved
criteria.fix: Approve changes explicitly when you review them.
criteria.why: An explicit approval records that someone accepted the change, not just that it was looked at.

criteria.text: Agent permissions are committed: is true
criteria.title: Agent permissions are committed
criteria.fix: Commit a deny rule for an action no agent should take, such as `"deny": ["Bash(git push origin main)"]` under `permissions` in `.claude/settings.json`. It holds under auto mode too. If your organisation sets this centrally, run with --managed-settings.
criteria.why: Deny rules and hooks keep an agent inside its limits in every permission mode, auto mode included. Committed to the repository or set in managed settings, they apply the same way to everyone and are reviewed like code.

criteria.text: Agent hooks are committed: is true
criteria.title: Agent hooks are committed
criteria.fix: Commit the hooks that run checks around agent actions.
criteria.why: Committed hooks run around an agent's actions on every clone, so a check written once applies without the agent having to remember it.

criteria.text: Agent routines are committed: is true
criteria.title: Agent routines are committed
criteria.fix: Commit the routines agents run on a schedule or trigger.
criteria.why: Committed routines define the agent work the repository runs on a schedule or trigger, so it runs the same way each time and is reviewed like code.

criteria.text: Share of mapped docs outrun by their code: is at most 50
criteria.title: Most mapped docs keep pace with their code
criteria.fix: Refresh the docs the report lists under doc freshness.
criteria.why: An agent reads the docs as true. A doc whose code has moved on misleads it about that code.

criteria.text: Share of mapped docs outrun by their code: is at most 20
criteria.title: Four in five mapped docs keep pace
criteria.fix: Refresh the docs the report lists under doc freshness, oldest first.
criteria.why: With four in five mapped docs keeping pace with their code, an agent can take most of what it reads at its word.

criteria.text: Share of configured gates an instruction file states: is at least 50
criteria.title: Half the configured gates are stated
criteria.fix: Add the ready one-line snippet the report gives for each unstated gate to CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. Then the next session knows the rule before it meets the gate.
criteria.why: A gate an agent does not know about turns its job red after the work is done. Stated with its threshold, the gate is a constraint it can plan for.

criteria.text: Share of configured gates an instruction file states: is at least 100
criteria.title: Every configured gate is stated
criteria.fix: Add the remaining snippets the report gives, one line per gate: its rule, its threshold and the command that checks it before pushing.
criteria.why: With every configured gate written down, rule and threshold, an agent can check each one before it pushes.

criteria.text: Commands and thresholds the agent systems disagree on: is 0
criteria.title: Every agent system names the same checks
criteria.fix: Make the instruction files agree. Name the same test and lint commands and the same thresholds in each. Or replace each tool's file with the pointer line the report gives.
criteria.why: When agent systems are told different check commands or thresholds, one agent's change passes checks another agent was told to run differently.

criteria.text: Agent systems not linked to the canonical instruction file: is 0
criteria.title: Every agent system reads one canonical file
criteria.fix: Keep AGENTS.md as the one source. Make each other tool's file a short pointer or a symlink to it, with the exact line the report gives for that tool.
criteria.why: One source of instructions keeps every agent's picture of the repository the same, and keeps it maintained in one place.

criteria.text: Skill and agent files that break a disclosure rule: is 0
criteria.title: Skills load only what the task needs
criteria.fix: For each file the report names, fix the rule it breaks. Give each SKILL.md and agent definition a name, and a description of at most 1024 characters. Move detail that only some tasks need into references/, linked from SKILL.md. Link each reference to a file that exists.
criteria.why: A skill loads its whole SKILL.md every time it triggers, so detail that only one branch needs spends an agent's context before work starts; keeping the body small, the description within its limit and references one level deep keeps that cost to what the task uses.

criteria.text: Skills whose scripts have no tests beside them: is 0
criteria.title: Each skill's scripts have tests beside them (presence, not coverage)
criteria.fix: Add tests for each named skill's scripts in that skill's own folder (tests/ or test_*.py beside them); where the report finds them elsewhere, move or copy them in, since tests outside the folder do not ship with the skill.
criteria.why: A skill's scripts run with an agent's permissions every time it triggers; tests beside them are the only check that a change still does what the SKILL.md promises.

criteria.text: Skill and agent files holding a detected kind of personal data: is 0
criteria.title: No skill file holds a detected kind of personal data (email, phone, home path, IP, SSH login, credential, key)
criteria.fix: In each file the report names, remove the kind of data it lists, or replace it with a placeholder (user@example.com, /home/user/); a key or credential that was committed should also be rotated.
criteria.why: Skill text is loaded into every session that triggers it and copied wherever it is published, so personal data in it leaks to every user.

criteria.text: A contributing guide is committed: is true
criteria.title: A newcomer can learn how to send a change
criteria.fix: Commit a CONTRIBUTING.md that says how to build, test and shape a change, at the root, in .github/ or in docs/.
criteria.why: A contributing guide tells a newcomer, human or agent, how to build, test and shape a change the way the project merges it, and a security policy gives them a private route for a vulnerability instead of a public issue.

criteria.text: A security policy is committed or shared by the owner: is true
criteria.title: A newcomer can report a vulnerability privately
criteria.fix: Commit a SECURITY.md that says how to report a vulnerability privately, at the root, in .github/ or in docs/, or link GitHub private vulnerability reporting.
criteria.why: A contributing guide tells a newcomer, human or agent, how to build, test and shape a change the way the project merges it, and a security policy gives them a private route for a vulnerability instead of a public issue.

tags.title: Behaviour
tags.why: That the code's behaviour is checked by something that runs on every change, not taken on trust.

tags.title: Contracts
tags.why: That generated output and its source agree, so an agent editing one does not quietly break the other.

tags.title: Docs
tags.why: That what an agent reads about the code is still true of the code.

tags.title: Structure
tags.why: That the code is shaped so an agent can work on one part without holding the whole repository in mind.

tags.title: Agent context
tags.why: That an agent starts each task knowing how this repository works and how to check its own change.

tags.title: Agent runtime
tags.why: That an agent can see the system it changes run, and confirm a change there, not only in the code.

tags.title: Governance
tags.why: That people stay in the loop on what agents change, and that what agents may do is agreed and visible.

tags.title: Supply chain
tags.why: That an agent builds and tests against the same dependency versions as CI and everyone else.

scans.why: Committed allowlists, hooks, sandbox rules and routines make an agent's limits and repeated work the same on every clone, and reviewable like code.

scans.name: coverage_gate
scans.title: Coverage gate
scans.summary: Finds coverage thresholds written in CI, task-runner and tool config, each with its file, line and threshold.

unknown_reasons.means: A go.mod or Cargo.toml has no coverage gate found for it. No gate of at least 50 percent exists for another language either (a low Python gate beside go.mod is not unmet). Its gate may be a script that compares go tool cover (or a report) to a number, which this scan does not read.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change if a script gates coverage. To have it measured, set the threshold in go-test-coverage's .testcoverage.yml, cargo tarpaulin --fail-under or cargo llvm-cov --fail-under-lines.

unknown_reasons.means: The only coverage gate that could reach 50 percent is a Codecov project status. Its target is auto, missing (Codecov's default is auto) or not a number. So the floor it holds is the base commit's coverage, not a number this scan can compare.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Run a coverage threshold of at least 50 percent in a CI step, such as pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80 or a fail_under your CI runs. A numeric Codecov target (target: 80%) makes the threshold readable. Whether branch protection requires the status is not read.

unknown_reasons.means: The only coverage gate that could reach 50 percent is a Codecov patch status. It bounds coverage of the changed lines only, and removing a test changes none, so it says nothing about the floor on total coverage.
unknown_reasons.next_step: To have the coverage gate measured, run a coverage threshold of at least 50 percent in a CI step. Examples are pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80, or a fail_under your CI runs. Or add a numeric target to a Codecov project status.

unknown_reasons.means: The coverage gate of at least 50 percent is a Codecov status target, and no CI line runs it. Codecov posts it as a commit status. It holds a merge only when branch protection requires it, and this scan does not read branch protection.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change if the Codecov status is a required check. To have the coverage gate measured, also run the threshold in a CI step (pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=80).

unknown_reasons.means: A scoped run found a fail_under in the root coverage.py config for a Python package with none of its own, not where CI runs coverage. coverage.py reads the config of the directory it runs in. So the root floor counts only when CI runs coverage from the root or names that config.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Run coverage in CI from the repository root (pytest --cov, coverage report), or pass the root config with --cov-config or --rcfile; or give the package its own fail_under and run coverage from its directory or with --cov-config naming that config.

scans.why: It finds the coverage threshold the repository sets and whether CI enforces it, which is the line that keeps tests from thinning out under a run of changes.

scans.name: units
scans.title: Monorepo units
scans.summary: The repository's units. First each skill folder (a SKILL.md), and a plugin's agents/ and commands/. Then the shallowest build-manifest folders, with each workspace root's declared members in its place, or the [[units]] of .assess/config.toml. Folders with only a manifest are skipped.
scans.why: One score for a monorepo describes none of its services. Naming each unit lets every one be scored on its own, so one service's gaps are not hidden behind another's practices.

scans.name: instruction_claims
scans.title: Instruction claims
scans.why: An agent trusts its instruction file without checking it. This checks each claim that a script runs in CI, a version is pinned or a count holds, and names the line of each that no longer does.

scans.name: claude_config
scans.title: Claude Code configuration
scans.why: Claude Code drops a frontmatter field it does not recognise without an error, so a skill, command or agent can look configured while doing nothing; this names each dropped field.

scans.name: nested_instructions
scans.title: Nested instruction files
scans.why: It measures the instruction text Claude Code loads on every task and the nested files it loads per directory, so the always-loaded part stays small enough for the rules in it to be followed.

scans.name: agent_harness
scans.title: Committed agent harness
scans.why: Committed hooks, env blocks and MCP servers run in every agent session, headless ones included; this lists what they run and flags any that expose a secret or widen an agent's reach.

scans.name: agent_environment
scans.title: Agent working environment
scans.summary: Committed agent setup, the check command an instruction file names, lockfiles per manifest, and the CI cap. The CI-duration probe is off in headless runs. A manifest row's note is skipped_library or direct_pins_only. skipped_library is a library whose ecosystem commits no lock: it is listed, and not counted in manifests_total or unlocked_total. direct_pins_only is a Gradle version catalog or NuGet central package management with no lock: it counts as unlocked.
scans.why: It reads what an agent needs to work like CI does: the check command its instructions name, the committed setup and a lockfile for each dependency manifest.

scans.title: Shared tooling

scans.name: review_automation
scans.title: AI review committed in CI
scans.why: A review step committed in CI reviews every change it runs on, and is evidence a headless run can read without platform access.

scans.name: review_evidence
scans.title: Review evidence
scans.summary: An AI review step committed in CI, or a reviewed merged change.

unknown_reasons.means: No AI review step is committed in CI, and a headless run without --platform makes no GitHub or GitLab read.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Run fleet or assess_signals.py with --platform, or /assess, with gh or glab signed in.

unknown_reasons.means: No AI review step is committed in CI and the repository has no GitHub or GitLab remote, so there are no merged changes to read.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change if the repository is local only; with a GitHub or GitLab remote, /assess and fleet --platform read its merged changes.

scans.why: It records whether changes get a second reader at all, from a committed AI review step or a reviewed merged change, so review is credited where it happens.

scans.name: ci_checks
scans.title: CI runs a test or lint command
scans.summary: Whether a GitHub Actions or GitLab CI line runs a test or lint command. Whether such a line can fail its job on ordinary changes: not masked, and not outside the ordinary triggers. Whether such a line runs a linter. The value is null when no check is found but a CI file pulls its jobs from elsewhere. It is also null when no check is found and the tree tracks a CI file the scan does not parse. It is null under --platform when most sampled merged pull requests carry an external CI check. It is null when a root Prow OWNERS_ALIASES is the only CI evidence.

unknown_reasons.means: A CI file pulls its jobs from a file this checkout does not hold, so the check may live there.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change: this reads as not measured until the included file can be read. On GitLab, fleet --platform reads the merged configuration through the CI lint API.

unknown_reasons.means: GitLab's merged CI configuration was read and runs no check, but jobs may be missing from it. The lint API does not expand an include under rules: or a trigger: child pipeline.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change: a check in a conditional include or child pipeline is not read, so this stays not measured rather than reading false.

unknown_reasons.means: In enforced_basis: an unmasked check sits in a workflow or job whose triggers this reader cannot settle. Examples are a missing on: key, or a rules: if: on a custom variable.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change if it runs on every change; naming push or pull_request, or a merge request rule, lets the scan read it.

unknown_reasons.means: In enforced_basis and lint_basis: the check's exit status may not reach its job. Causes are a || fallback that can pass (pytest || echo failed), an if or while condition, or an until loop that breaks. Or a check sits before && with more of the step after it, or in a { } group or function.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Let the check's exit status reach the step. Run the check on its own line, or end the fallback with exit 1 (pytest || { echo failed; exit 1; }).

unknown_reasons.means: In enforced_basis and lint_basis: the only CI line that would settle the signal runs a committed script (./ci.sh, bash scripts/test.sh, ./scripts/lint.sh). No tracked file matches that script, so it is not credited. An earlier step may still create it.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Commit the script the CI step runs. Or call the test or lint command in its own CI step (pytest, ruff check .), so the scan can read it.

unknown_reasons.means: No CI line runs the linter (lint_basis) or the check (enforced_basis). But one runs a target whose recipe is not read, and that target may run it. Examples: make check or npm test for a linter; make foo, npm run foo or ./scripts/foo.sh for a check.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change if the target runs the check; calling the test or lint command in its own CI step (make test, pytest, ruff check .) lets the scan read it.

unknown_reasons.means: No readable GitHub Actions or GitLab CI line settles the signal. The tree tracks a CI file of a system this scan does not parse, such as Jenkins, CircleCI, Azure Pipelines, Buildkite, LUCI, Prow or Zuul. The lib/unread_ci.py docstring lists the paths, and unread_ci_files counts them.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change: the scanner cannot read those systems' configuration, so their checks read as not measured rather than absent.

unknown_reasons.means: Under --platform only: no readable CI line settles the signal. Over half of sampled merged pull requests carry a check run or status from a known external CI system (Buildkite, LUCI, Prow tide, Azure Pipelines). A check ran; that earns no credit.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change: the checks run on a CI system configured outside the repository, so they read as not measured rather than absent.

unknown_reasons.means: The tree tracks no CI file of any kind, and the root holds a Prow OWNERS_ALIASES file. So presubmits likely run on Prow, configured in another repository. An OWNERS file alone is not a marker.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change: run with --platform to read the checks on merged pull requests instead.

unknown_reasons.means: In lint_basis: no CI line runs a linter, but a CI dotnet build runs the analysers a committed Directory.Build.props or .csproj turns on (EnforceCodeStyleInBuild, AnalysisLevel). Their severities live in .editorconfig, which the scan does not evaluate.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Nothing to change if the analysers fail the build on a finding; a CI step running dotnet format --verify-no-changes lets the scan read a lint run.

unknown_reasons.means: In lint_basis: no CI line runs a linter, and the only static gate is a compiler run with warnings as errors. Examples are mix compile --warnings-as-errors, -Werror, dotnet build -warnaserror and TreatWarningsAsErrors in Directory.Build.props. It is not counted as a lint run.
unknown_reasons.next_step: Running a linter or analyser in its own CI step (mix credo, clang-tidy, dotnet format --verify-no-changes) lets the scan read a lint run.

scans.why: It reads whether CI runs tests or linters on ordinary changes in a way that can stop the job, so "it passed" means a check ran and could have said no.

scans.name: instruction_placement
scans.title: Instruction placement
scans.why: It names the always-loaded sections that are reference for one tool or subtree, so they can move to files an agent reads when needed and leave the always-loaded text for rules.

scans.name: skill_disclosure
scans.title: Skill disclosure
scans.summary: Each SKILL.md and agent definition against Anthropic's skill authoring guidance: body lines, size in tokens, name and description, and references that resolve one level deep.
scans.why: A skill loads its whole SKILL.md every time it triggers, so detail that only one branch needs spends an agent's context before work starts; keeping the body small, the description within its limit and references one level deep keeps that cost to what the task uses.

scans.name: skill_script_tests
scans.title: Skill script tests
scans.summary: Whether each skill's scripts have tests beside them in the skill's own folder: presence, not coverage, since no suite runs. Tests found only outside the folder are named, as information.
scans.why: A skill's scripts run with an agent's permissions every time it triggers; tests beside them are the only check that a change still does what the SKILL.md promises.

scans.name: skill_personal_data
scans.title: Personal data in skill text

findings.name: hidden_coupling
findings.title: Hidden coupling
findings.action: check why these files change together
findings.why: These files change together in history with no import between them, so an agent changing one has nothing in the code telling it to change the other.

findings.name: lying_map
findings.title: Stale doc over complex code
findings.why: The doc has fallen behind complex code it describes, which is where an agent leans on a doc most.

findings.name: unexplained_complexity
findings.title: Unexplained complexity
findings.action: write the contract the code needs (write it by hand; do not generate it)
findings.why: Complex code with no doc of what it should do leaves an agent only the code to infer intent from, so it cannot tell a bug from a requirement.

findings.name: untrusted_hotspot
findings.title: Untrusted hotspot
findings.action: make the tests check what the code does, as a caller sees it (not its internal state)
findings.why: Complex, often-changed code whose tests let many mutants survive: an agent's change here is not held by the tests that look like they cover it.

findings.name: self_referential_tests
findings.title: Self-referential tests
findings.action: ask a person to review: the tests check that the code agrees with itself, not that it is right
findings.why: Tests kept and committed beside the code they cover can check internal consistency rather than truth, so an agent changing both together can make them agree on a wrong answer.

findings.name: unactioned_intent
findings.title: Unactioned intent
findings.action: keep the promise: fix it, open a ticket for it, or delete the marker or skip
findings.why: A TODO or skip that survives many edits reads to an agent as a live plan or a settled exception, and it cannot tell which.

findings.name: accretion_ratchet
findings.title: Accretion ratchet
findings.action: make the file smaller: move code out, delete dead code, or split the file
findings.why: A file that has only ever grown gets harder to read whole with each change, and each agent addition makes the next one harder.

findings.name: orphaned_understanding
findings.title: Orphaned understanding
findings.action: name a person who owns this code before it changes again
findings.why: Complex code with no human author and no doc of its intent has nobody to ask and nothing to check an agent's reading against.

findings.name: candidate_dead_weight
findings.title: Candidate dead weight
findings.action: check that the code is used, and delete it if it is not
findings.why: Code nothing in the repository calls costs an agent reading time and can be maintained by mistake; it needs a person to confirm no outside caller uses it.

findings.name: override_contradicts_signals
findings.title: Archetype override contradicts the signals
findings.action: Review the archetype marker: the measured signals suggest a different kind of repository
findings.why: The declared repository kind decides which checks apply; when the signals disagree, checks marked not applicable may hide gaps an agent would meet.

findings.name: refactor_boundary
findings.title: Refactor boundary
findings.action: safe to hand an agent in isolation
findings.why: A strength: edits here stay inside the directory, so an agent can change it without reading the rest of the repository.
